A2.text:
Leyla and her husband Murad lived in the busy centre of Baku. Murad hated his long daily commute. He sat in slow traffic for two hours every day.

“I am so tired of this noisy city,” Murad said one evening. “I want a peaceful life. Let's buy a small rural house in Quba.”

Leyla agreed. On Saturday morning, they drove to Quba to look at a beautiful stone house. The garden was amazing. There were many tall apple trees, and the air was very clean.

“It is perfect,” Murad smiled. “We can drink tea here every morning.”

Suddenly, the weather changed. A heavy storm started, and the electricity stopped working. They sat in the dark living room for four hours. It was very cold. Leyla tried to watch a funny video on her phone, but there was no internet connection.

“Maybe it is too quiet here,” Murad said. He looked at his wife and laughed.

The next morning, they quickly drove back to Baku. When Leyla saw the tall buildings of the city, she felt very happy.

“I love the city,” she said. “But we need a quieter place.”

A month later, they did not move to Quba. Instead, they bought a house in a quiet suburb of Baku. It had a small garden, and the internet was very fast.

questions.q: What is the story mainly about?
options: A husband and wife who decide country life is not for them yet
A couple who get lost in a forest
How to buy a cheap house in Baku
A dangerous storm that destroys a village
questions.why: They want to move to a rural house, but after a boring and cold storm, they decide to buy a house in a suburb instead.

questions.q: How much time did Murad spend traveling to work every day?
questions.why: “He sat in slow traffic for two hours every day.”

questions.q: What did Leyla try to do when the electricity stopped working?
options: Watch a video on her phone
questions.why: “Leyla tried to watch a funny video on her phone, but there was no internet connection.”

questions.q: The stone house in Quba did not have a garden.
questions.why: The text says, “The garden was amazing. There were many tall apple trees...”

questions.q: The story says they want to move to a “suburb”. What does this word mean?
options: A busy city centre with tall buildings
A residential area outside the city centre
questions.why: They didn't move to rural Quba, but chose a quiet area just outside Baku (a suburb) to have a garden and fast internet.

questions.q: Why did Murad laugh when he said, “Maybe it is too quiet here”?
options: He was listening to a funny joke
He was happy the storm stopped
He realised they were bored and missed the city
questions.why: They were sitting in the dark and cold with no internet, realising their dream of a peaceful rural life was actually boring and difficult.

B1.text:
Leyla and her husband Murad lived in a small flat in the busy centre of Baku. Murad was completely exhausted from the urban overcrowding and his terrible morning commute. Every day, he spent two hours sitting in heavy traffic just to get to his office.

“I cannot do this anymore,” Murad sighed one Friday evening. “I need a peaceful life away from the city. Let's look for a rural property in Quba. We can grow our own vegetables.”

Leyla thought it was a wonderful idea. The next weekend, they drove up to the mountains to view an old stone cottage. It had huge apple trees and plenty of beautiful green space.

“This is exactly what we need,” Murad said, breathing in the fresh air. “Imagine having breakfast here.”

But later that afternoon, a dark storm rolled over the mountains. The wind blew hard, and the electricity immediately went out. They soon discovered that the local infrastructure was quite poor. They sat in the freezing living room for five hours, wrapped in thick blankets. Leyla tried to check her work emails, but her phone had no signal at all.

“You know,” Murad whispered in the dark, “maybe I like electricity more than fresh air.”

The following morning, they packed their bags and drove back down the mountain. As they got closer to the city, the famous Baku skyline appeared in the distance. Leyla smiled brightly. She had never been so happy to see traffic lights and coffee shops.

In the end, they compromised. They gave up on the mountain cottage and moved to a quiet suburb just outside Baku. It gave them a lovely garden to relax in, but they were still close enough to enjoy city life — and high-speed internet.

questions.q: Why did Leyla and Murad decide not to buy the mountain cottage?
options: The house was too expensive for them
Murad lost his job in the city
They realized they were not ready to live without modern comforts
The owner did not want to sell the house
questions.why: After spending hours in the cold without electricity or signal, they realise they prefer having city amenities.

questions.q: What did Murad want to do at the rural property?
questions.why: “Let's look for a rural property in Quba. We can grow our own vegetables.”

questions.q: Why couldn't Leyla check her work emails during the storm?
options: She left her phone in Baku
Murad asked her not to work
questions.why: “Leyla tried to check her work emails, but her phone had no signal at all.”

questions.q: Leyla and Murad sold their flat in Baku before traveling to Quba.
questions.why: The text says they lived in a small flat and drove to Quba for the weekend, but it never mentions if they sold their flat first.

questions.q: Murad was tired of the “overcrowding”. What does this word mean?
options: When a place is too expensive
When the weather is very hot
When a city has no trees
When there are too many people in one place
questions.why: He is exhausted by the busy centre, heavy traffic, and too many people, which defines overcrowding.

questions.q: How did Leyla feel when she saw the traffic lights and coffee shops?
options: Angry because she hated the city
Relieved and excited to be back in civilisation
Sad that the weekend was over
Nervous about driving in the traffic
questions.why: “Leyla smiled brightly. She had never been so happy to see traffic lights and coffee shops.”

B2.text:
For five years, Leyla and her husband Murad had lived in a cramped apartment right in the bustling heart of Baku. Recently, the urban overcrowding had started to take its toll on them both. Murad, in particular, was burnt out from the daily commute, spending over two hours a day crawling through gridlocked traffic just to reach his office.

“I am so done with this rat race,” Murad announced one Friday, dropping his briefcase on the sofa. “I want to put down roots somewhere peaceful. Let's buy a rural farmhouse in Quba. We can escape the noise and actually hear ourselves think.”

Drawn to the romantic idea of country living, Leyla agreed. The very next weekend, they drove up into the misty mountains of Quba to view a charming stone cottage. It boasted a vast orchard of apple trees and offered more green space than they had ever seen.

“This is paradise,” Murad beamed, taking a deep breath of the crisp autumn air. “Imagine waking up to this silence every single day.”

However, the silence was soon broken by a fierce thunderstorm. As heavy rain battered the roof, the power grid failed, plunging the house into darkness. They quickly realised that the rural infrastructure left a lot to be desired. Wrapped in heavy woollen blankets, they shivered in the freezing living room for six hours. When Leyla tried to stream a film to pass the time, she found her phone had absolutely no reception.

“I have to admit,” Murad muttered through chattering teeth, “I might actually prefer central heating over scenic views.”

They packed their bags at dawn and fled back down the winding mountain roads. When the familiar, glittering Baku skyline finally came into view, Leyla let out a long sigh of relief. She had never felt so grateful for concrete, streetlights, and twenty-four-hour supermarkets.

Ultimately, they reached a sensible compromise. Instead of fleeing to the wilderness, they bought a spacious house in a leafy suburb on the edge of the city. It gave them a tranquil garden and fresh air, but kept them firmly connected to civilisation — and, crucially, fibre-optic internet.

words.phrase: left a lot to be desired

questions.q: What is the main theme of Leyla and Murad's experience?
options: The romantic idea of country living often clashes with harsh reality
Buying a house in the city is a better financial investment
Couples should never travel during thunderstorm season
Working in an office is better than working on a farm
questions.why: They loved the idea of a peaceful farmhouse, but hated the reality of freezing temperatures and no internet, leading them to compromise.

questions.q: How did Murad describe his daily journey to the office?
options: Driving too fast on the motorway
questions.why: “...spending over two hours a day crawling through gridlocked traffic just to reach his office.”

questions.q: What did Leyla try to do while they were shivering in the living room?
options: Stream a film on her phone
Light a fire in the chimney
Cook dinner on a gas stove
questions.why: “When Leyla tried to stream a film to pass the time, she found her phone had absolutely no reception.”

questions.q: Murad and Leyla completely abandoned their plan to leave the city centre.
questions.why: False. They didn't stay in the centre; they “bought a spacious house in a leafy suburb on the edge of the city.”

questions.q: Murad says he is done with the “rat race”. What does this idiom mean?
options: A problem with pests in an old building
A sporting event held in the capital
A slow and relaxing daily routine
questions.why: The phrase refers to the tiring, endless struggle for wealth or power in city life, which he wants to escape.

questions.q: Why did Murad say he might prefer central heating over scenic views?
options: Because he thought the cottage was ugly
Because he wanted to save money on electricity
Because he was freezing and realised natural beauty couldn't keep him warm
Because he works for a heating company
questions.why: He said it “through chattering teeth” while shivering in the dark, showing he valued basic comfort more than the beautiful nature outside.

podcast.title: A rooster at six

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Do you live in a city or a village? Guess: what woke Sam up at six in the morning in the countryside?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is city versus countryside. And I've just come back from a weekend in a village!
[laugh] My grandparents' village, in the mountains. Tell everyone what happened at six in the morning.
A rooster! Right under my window. In the city I wake up to buses. There, I woke up to a very loud bird.
That's rural life. But you liked it, didn't you?
I loved it. It was so peaceful. No traffic, no noise — just mountains, fresh bread and a lot of tea.
My grandmother made you eat three breakfasts.
[chuckle] Four. Then I came back to Baku on Monday, and it was the opposite — traffic, crowds and my long commute to work.
How long is your commute?
About an hour each way. Sometimes I feel stuck in the rat race — work, metro, sleep, repeat.
But the city has good things too. Urban life means jobs, universities, hospitals, cinemas. In my grandparents' village, the nearest hospital is forty minutes away.
That's true. The infrastructure is better in the city — roads, fast internet, public transport.
But big cities have problems too. Overcrowding is a big one. Some parts of Baku have new buildings everywhere and not enough green space.
I agree. A city needs parks. When I look at the skyline from the seaside, it's beautiful, but I also want trees.
So what's the answer? A suburb? A house a little outside the city, with a garden?
Maybe. Half city, half countryside. Close enough to work, quiet enough to sleep.
My parents did that. They moved to a suburb when I was twelve, and they put down roots there. They know every neighbour now.
That's what I'd like one day — to put down roots somewhere and grow my own tomatoes.
[laugh] You? Tomatoes?
Why not? Your grandmother showed me how. I'm a fast learner.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: would you rather live in a big city or in the countryside — and why?
The countryside — but without the rooster. See you next time!
Bye for now!

options: The good and bad sides of city and village life
questions.why: Sam's weekend in a village starts a talk about city, countryside and suburbs.

options: Settle in a place and make it your home
questions.why: Leyla's parents stayed in the suburb and know every neighbour.

questions.q: Where would Sam probably like to live?
options: In the busiest part of the city
In a quiet place near the city, with a garden
In a village far from any city
questions.why: "Half city, half countryside… grow my own tomatoes."
